task.goal: Create a low-pressure way for a repair café to celebrate failed repair attempts as useful learning rather than shame.
hard_constraints: Four volunteers have a table, paper and a small display board for one monthly event.
No photos or names without explicit consent, no prizes or leaderboards, and no unsafe repair advice.
Participation is optional, usable without public speaking, and does not slow the queue substantially; pilot with observation and opt-out checks.
task.available_resources: Existing repair notes with permission to summarize anonymously.
task.expected_result: A concrete ritual and evaluation of learning versus embarrassment.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A Useful Ending
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make an unsuccessful repair produce a small, optional learning record. The mechanism is to give the attempt a useful endpoint: an observation or boundary worth remembering, even when the item remains broken.

At handback, a volunteer offers a paper slip: “Still broken; now we know…” The owner can tick “one possibility ruled out,” “a limit identified,” “a question clarified,” or “nothing clear yet,” then optionally add a sentence. No explanation aloud is required. Blank slips are fine. The owner keeps the slip unless they separately consent to an anonymous summary appearing on the board. A volunteer reviews any shared wording, removing identifying details and procedural repair advice. The board heading reads “Useful endings this month.” Permitted existing notes can supply a few examples without implying that their owners joined this ritual.

Four volunteers use one table corner for slips and the small board for summaries. The handback volunteer makes the offer; another reviews contributions during quiet moments. Folding paper creates separate collection pockets for publication consent and private feedback. Participation should take under a minute away from the service queue.

This assumes some visitors value a concrete record of what changed. It may feel forced when nothing useful emerged, so “nothing clear yet” must remain an equally acceptable ending. The ritual celebrates careful inquiry without claiming every failure is beneficial.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: During one event, alternate short handback periods offering either an ordinary repair summary or that summary plus the optional slip. In both periods, offer anonymous exit ticks: “I learned something useful: yes/unsure/no” and “The handback made me feel embarrassed or pressured: yes/unsure/no.” A volunteer observes handback time and whether declined offers are accepted immediately, without recording identities. Inspect whether completed slips contain a specific observation rather than compulsory positivity. The idea is weakened if learning responses resemble the comparator while embarrassment, pressure, or delays increase. Low response numbers and self-selection limit conclusions; do not treat uptake as proof of comfort.

DIRECT_FULL.title: The Open Questions Board
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Celebrate failed attempts by treating them as contributions to the café’s shared understanding of uncertainty. The mechanism is collective sense-making: an unresolved item can reveal a recurring question worth investigating, without putting its owner on display.

Before the event, volunteers turn permitted repair notes into three or four anonymous, non-procedural questions, such as “What information was missing before diagnosis?” or “When did we recognize that this repair exceeded our facilities?” Each card includes an honest statement of what remains unknown. Avoid item descriptions that could identify someone.

Visitors may silently read the board, place a pencil mark beside a question that helped them understand their own visit, or submit a new question on paper. Nothing requires describing their repair publicly. New submissions need a separate publication-consent tick and volunteer review. The closing ritual is a handwritten board footer: “These questions are worth carrying forward,” followed by one or two questions selected for relevance and safe scope, without vote totals or rankings. No promise of a future answer is made.

One volunteer prepares the initial cards, one checks proposed additions during quiet periods, and all four continue their ordinary repair roles. Reading and marking happen at the table edge after handback, outside the queue.

This assumes shared uncertainty can reduce isolation and support learning. It could instead resemble a catalogue of inadequacy or invite speculative technical advice. Keep all cards about observations, information needs, and service limits; omit repair instructions and unsupported explanations.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Display the same permitted note summaries first as plain anonymous accounts and then as open questions, switching order midway through the event if practical. Offer separate optional paper responses: “What, if anything, did this help you understand?” and “Did this display make failed repairs feel more acceptable, unchanged, or more uncomfortable?” Observe congestion and whether visitors can bypass it easily. Compare the specificity of learning responses and reported discomfort between versions. The mechanism is doubtful if questions generate only vague approval, greater discomfort, or unsafe advice submissions. Different visitors and time periods make this a small design check, not causal proof.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Thank the Care, Leave the Outcome
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use a private acknowledgment ritual to separate appreciation of a repair attempt from whether it succeeded. The mechanism is relational: a visitor can feel respected when someone recognizes a specific act of care, without having to reinterpret disappointment as success.

At handback, a volunteer may offer a folded paper card: “Would you like a short acknowledgment of the attempt? Passing is fine.” Inside, the volunteer writes one truthful, observable contribution, such as “You explained the fault clearly” or “We stopped when we reached the limits of our equipment.” Avoid praising persistence indiscriminately, assigning blame, or implying that stopping proves a repair was safe. The visitor can keep, decline, or discard it without explanation. There is no public reading.

A separate optional slip asks, “What care or effort would you like this café to recognize?” Visitors may acknowledge listening, patience, clear explanations, or respecting a decision to stop. With explicit permission, volunteers summarize these themes anonymously on the board under “Care we noticed today.” The board contains neither identifiable repair stories nor individual credits. This makes celebration visible while keeping personal acknowledgment private.

Four volunteers agree on a few factual wording examples before opening. Cards are completed only when handback allows; otherwise a visitor can take a blank reflection card to the table. One volunteer checks board contributions during a lull. Existing notes are unnecessary.

The approach assumes recognition feels supportive. It may seem patronizing, especially after a frustrating visit, and it does not itself establish technical learning. The offer must be brief, sincere, and easy to refuse.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare ordinary handbacks with handbacks offering the private acknowledgment during alternating short periods. Give both groups optional anonymous exit questions: “I felt respected,” “I can name something learned or a limit clarified,” and “I felt expected to be positive,” each with yes/unsure/no options. Observe added handback time, repeated offers after refusal, and any queue obstruction. A useful result would combine respect with identifiable learning or clearer limits, without increased pressure. Reject or revise the ritual if appreciation rises but pressure also rises, or if visitors describe it as patronizing. Sparse feedback leaves uncertainty; silence and acceptance are not evidence of comfort.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Volunteers Go First
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make volunteers’ own unsuccessful attempts visible before inviting any visitor contribution. The mechanism is norm-setting through example: when the people treated as experts acknowledge uncertainty and disappointment without self-mockery, visitors may feel less personally judged by an unsuccessful repair.

Before opening, each willing volunteer writes a short anonymous account of an attempt they personally made: “We hoped… / What happened… / What changed in our understanding…” Use only truthful accounts they consent to share. Include unresolved disappointment where appropriate; do not manufacture a lesson. Exclude identifying item details, repair instructions, and claims that an item is safe. Two accounts are enough if others prefer to pass.

Display these under “Our attempts sometimes end here too.” At handback, a volunteer can briefly point out that the board is optional reading, without asking the visitor to contribute or respond. Beside it, provide folded paper headed “Something I wish repair volunteers understood about an unsuccessful visit.” Visitors can deposit an anonymous private note without speaking. These notes remain private and are not added to the display.

During a quiet moment near closing, the four volunteers read the notes and write one collective acknowledgment on the board, such as “A disappointing outcome can still deserve a clear explanation.” This closes the ritual without displaying visitors’ experiences or requiring positive feelings.

The table, paper, and board suffice; preparation takes a few minutes, and reading happens beyond the queue. The approach assumes volunteer examples feel credible and relatable. It could instead undermine confidence or make visitors feel responsible for comforting volunteers. Keep accounts brief, avoid excuses, and never seek reassurance.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Pilot during one event with alternating display periods: a neutral description of the café’s repair limits versus the volunteer accounts. Offer the same optional anonymous exit slip in both periods: “An unsuccessful repair would make me feel judged here: yes/unsure/no”; “Something this helped me understand: ___”; and “I felt asked to reassure volunteers: yes/unsure/no.” A volunteer observes queue obstruction and whether people can bypass the display and decline feedback without another invitation. Revise or stop if the accounts increase reported judgment, solicit comforting responses, or produce reassurance without identifiable learning. Different visitors, timing, and voluntary responses prevent a causal conclusion; uptake alone does not show comfort.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A Failed Attempt Changes Our Welcome
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Give unsuccessful attempts a concrete consequence in how the café operates. The mechanism is visible institutional responsiveness: an attempt becomes useful because the café changes a small practice in response, rather than asking its owner to find a positive meaning in the outcome.

Before the event, volunteers review existing repair notes that may be summarized anonymously. Choose one recurring, well-supported communication problem associated with unsuccessful visits—for example, visitors not knowing which equipment the café lacks. Do not infer a recurring problem from a single ambiguous note. Agree on one modest change achievable with paper, such as placing a plain-language facilities notice at the table.

Put a two-part card on the display board: “Earlier unsuccessful attempts showed us…” and “Today we changed…” Describe the communication gap and actual change without identifying visitors, blaming anyone, or giving technical repair advice. Label it “An attempt that changed the café.” This is the celebratory act: publicly crediting unsuccessful work with improving the service, without naming its participants or suggesting their disappointment was necessary.

After handback, anyone may silently leave a private slip completing “One thing that would have made today clearer…” Submission is optional and separate from service. A publication-consent box permits an anonymous summary, but private feedback remains useful without that permission. During a lull, volunteers may implement one feasible clarification and update the board only after doing so. If nothing suitable emerges, leave the original change visible rather than inventing progress.

All four volunteers retain their repair roles; one checks slips during quiet periods. This requires authority to make small communication changes and enough permitted notes to identify a genuine issue. It cannot compensate for a poor repair explanation, and the board could feel promotional unless it states the change modestly and honestly.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For a small prototype, alternate between displaying the new facilities notice alone and displaying it with the anonymous account of why it changed. Keep the actual service improvement available throughout. Offer optional exit ticks: “I understand this café’s limits”; “Unsuccessful attempts seem useful to improving this café”; and “This framing made my disappointment feel dismissed,” each with yes/unsure/no, plus space for an example of something learned. Observe congestion, unobstructed opt-out, and whether volunteers pursue declined feedback. The proposed mechanism is weakened if the origin story adds no understanding or usefulness, or increases dismissal. Inspect whether the promised change actually happened. One event provides a practical design check, with substantial uncertainty from small numbers and self-selection.

DIRECT_FULL.title: The Hindsight Fold
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Turn a permitted account of an unsuccessful repair into a silent, folded-paper exercise that lets visitors experience how uncertainty changes with information. The mechanism is perspective-taking: an outcome can look obvious afterward, while an honest reconstruction shows why the attempt was informative.

Before the event, two volunteers select one existing repair note with permission for anonymous summarization. It must document both an initial uncertainty and something the attempt actually established. If no note supports that sequence, do not manufacture one. Remove identifying details and all procedural repair advice.

The outside of a folded sheet gives the initial situation in broad terms and asks: “Could you tell whether a repair would be possible from this information?” Readers can privately consider “yes,” “no,” or “unsure,” without submitting an answer. Inside, reveal the documented outcome and the specific information gained. Include “The item remained unrepaired” plainly. The final line reads: “This attempt gave us a case worth learning from. Disappointment can remain.” There is no correct-answer score, public response, or invitation to diagnose the item.

Place a few copies at the table edge, clear of the queue. The board holds the same folded case under “An unsuccessful attempt, a useful lesson.” Opening the fold is the optional ritual; visitors need neither speak nor contribute their own experience. Two volunteers prepare and check the wording before opening; all four retain their ordinary roles during service.

This assumes the notes preserve enough information to reconstruct uncertainty faithfully. A selective account could excuse poor work or exaggerate learning. Use modest claims and omit cases whose educational value depends on technical instructions.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: During one event, alternate the folded version with an unfolded version containing exactly the same account. Offer optional anonymous slips asking: “What did this attempt establish?”, “Did this make unsuccessful repairs feel less shameful, unchanged, or more shameful?”, and “Did you feel tested or pressured?” Observe obstruction and whether visitors can ignore the display without prompting. Stop or revise if the fold attracts guessing but yields no clearer learning, increases embarrassment, or delays service. Sparse, self-selected feedback cannot establish effectiveness; inspect unanswered and critical responses alongside favorable ones.

EXPAND.title: The Volunteer Goes First
EXPAND.proposal:
Make fallibility visible through a volunteer’s own account of an unsuccessful attempt. The mechanism is social modeling: someone with an established helper role demonstrates that acknowledging a mistaken assumption does not cost belonging or respect.

Before opening, one willing volunteer prepares a short paper account of their own repair attempt: “I expected… / What actually happened… / What changed in my thinking…” Use only a truthful account the volunteer explicitly consents to display. Exclude identifying information about other people and all procedural repair instructions. If nobody wants to contribute, skip this route; do not substitute a visitor’s story.

Place the account on the small board under “Our helpers are learning too.” The ritual is a silent reading invitation at the table edge, available throughout the event. A final line says, “An unsuccessful attempt still belongs here. Disappointment belongs here too.” Visitors need not respond, disclose their own outcome, or speak publicly. An optional paper response asks which assumption changed, if any; it stays private unless separately approved for anonymous display.

One volunteer owns preparation and removal, another checks wording, and the other two maintain normal service. Reading happens outside the queue. If the featured volunteer withdraws consent or feels exposed, remove the account immediately without explanation.

This assumes perceived expert infallibility contributes to shame. It may fail when visitors interpret the account as evidence of poor competence. Unlike the prior private acknowledgment route, it changes what helpers publicly model rather than how they praise visitors.
EXPAND.experiment: Pilot one account during a monthly event. Compare short periods showing it with periods showing a simple acknowledgment of care, based on the prior route. Offer optional anonymous ticks: “I can identify something learned,” “My unsuccessful repair would feel acceptable here,” and “This reduced my confidence in the café.” Observe bypass access and queue interference. The display owner stops immediately for consent withdrawal, identifying details, or congestion. Do not retain the added preparation if learning and acceptance show no improvement, or confidence concerns increase. Small, self-selected responses can reveal problems but cannot establish an effect.

EXPAND.title: Choose, Reveal, Discuss Silently
EXPAND.proposal:
Turn an unsuccessful attempt into a brief exercise in deciding when to continue and when to hand off. The mechanism is judgment rehearsal: visitors make a choice before seeing the relevant service boundary, making the lesson more usable than simply reading a conclusion.

Two volunteers prepare three short, anonymous case cards from permitted notes where possible; clearly label any invented teaching scenario. Use a close pair: the same unresolved fault with a required qualified supervisor available versus unavailable. Explicitly state that all other café requirements are satisfied. Add an unfamiliar case involving an item outside the café’s accepted scope. Each card asks only “Continue within café rules, or stop and hand off?” A folded flap reveals the applicable café rule and the supported choice. Include no repair procedures, hazard diagnosis, or claim that these examples certify an actual item as safe. If volunteers cannot establish an unambiguous existing rule, omit that card.

At the table edge, visitors may privately choose, unfold, and check. Nobody submits a score. The board says, “An unsuccessful attempt helped us practise a better decision.” No rankings, public answers, or owner stories appear. Visitors can leave at any point.

One volunteer checks the rules, one checks anonymity and wording, one observes access during brief intervals, and one maintains service cover; all retain their ordinary roles. Stop offering the activity whenever staffing or queue conditions require it.

This assumes uncertainty about stopping contributes to shame or repeated overreach. Unlike the prior open-questions board, this route rehearses a decision and supplies bounded feedback. Its limit is transfer: recognizing a paper example does not establish competence in real repairs.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare the folded exercise with the same cases and rules displayed already answered. Optional anonymous slips record choices for the close pair and unfamiliar case, plus “This made me feel tested or embarrassed.” The activity owner checks whether choices follow the stated boundary, especially on the unfamiliar case, and observes dwell time and obstruction. Stop if visitors treat cards as repair authorization or the table blocks access. Prefer the simple answered display if rehearsal adds work without clearer choices, or increases embarrassment. Report sparse responses as inconclusive.

EXPAND.title: A Failure That Changed the Café
EXPAND.proposal:
Celebrate an unsuccessful repair by making one resulting improvement to the café visible. The mechanism is consequential follow-through: learning becomes credible when the organization changes something because of the attempt.

Before the event, two volunteers review permitted anonymous notes for a repeated, nontechnical service problem, such as visitors learning too late that a particular document is needed. Choose one small change within the four volunteers’ authority: for example, a paper arrival prompt that helps visitors identify relevant information before joining the queue. Do not change technical procedures, expand repair scope, or imply that the change guarantees repair success. If the notes support no feasible change, do not manufacture a lesson.

The board contains a three-part record: “An attempt remained unresolved / It exposed this service problem / Today we changed this.” Remove details that could identify an owner; obtain separate explicit consent if anonymity cannot be assured. Name no individual and display no photographs.

The ritual happens when the new practice is first used: the responsible volunteer adds “Now in use” to the board. Visitors may silently read or leave a private correction. Nobody must contribute their repair story or express gratitude. At closing, the owner adds an honest observation: helped, unclear, or withdrawn.

One volunteer owns the change, another checks privacy, and the remaining two continue service while all four retain normal roles. Withdraw the change if it creates confusion or delays.

This assumes visitors doubt whether unsuccessful attempts accomplish anything. Unlike the prior learning-slip route, the benefit is an observable organizational response rather than a personal statement. The risk is celebrating a cosmetic change or implying that a visitor’s inconvenience was justified.
EXPAND.experiment: For one event, compare a short period using ordinary handback learning slips with a period using the service change and its board record. Privately ask whether visitors can identify a useful lesson and whether they feel their disappointment was minimized. Separately observe whether the targeted service problem actually occurs less often and whether work shifts onto arrivals. The change owner stops for privacy concerns, longer queues, or repeated confusion. Reject the added ritual if visitors report no clearer learning than with slips, or the change adds burden without addressing its stated problem. Time-period differences limit attribution.

EXPAND.title: Put Unsuccessful Repairs in Context
EXPAND.proposal:
Reduce the sense that a failed repair marks someone as an exceptional failure by showing honest outcome context before handback. The mechanism is attribution through a denominator: visitors see that unresolved outcomes are an ordinary part of the service, alongside varied reasons, rather than evidence of personal inadequacy.

Before the event, two volunteers inspect a bounded set of existing notes whose permission covers anonymous aggregation. Define outcomes consistently: restored during the visit, partly improved, unresolved, and unclear. Display the total and all categories together, with the date range and “These records may not represent today’s visits.” Use broad, nontechnical reasons only when supported by the notes. Do not publish small breakdowns that could identify individuals. If permission, completeness, or privacy is inadequate, do not display statistics or invent estimates.

The small board sits beside the table where visitors can bypass it. Its invitation reads, “Every outcome can inform the next visit; nobody owes us a lesson.” At closing, a volunteer adds one supported, non-procedural takeaway from the reviewed records, such as a recurring information gap. This quiet update is the celebration; no visitor contributes publicly or is counted for a performance target.

One volunteer owns the tally and wording, another verifies it, and the other two keep normal service moving. Remove the board if visitors mistake the figures for promises or targets. No photographs, names, prizes, or repair advice appear.

This assumes shame partly comes from believing everyone else succeeds. Unlike the prior open-questions board, it changes perceived normality through outcome context. It may instead lower confidence or normalize avoidable service problems; the denominator must never excuse poor care.
EXPAND.experiment: During one event, alternate the context board with a similarly sized open-questions display. Offer optional anonymous exit ticks: “An unresolved repair would make me feel singled out,” “I learned something useful,” and “I felt the café was excusing poor service.” Observe bypass access and any added explanation time. The board owner stops for privacy concerns, misleading interpretations, or queue interference. Prefer the simpler questions display if context produces no clearer acceptance or learning after accounting for tallying effort, or increases distrust. Check that visitors can decline feedback without a repeated offer; nonresponse is not evidence of comfort.

EXPAND.title: Upgrade of P0: A Useful Ending, with an honest check
EXPAND.proposal:
Preserve P0’s mechanism: give an unsuccessful attempt a useful endpoint through a private learning slip. Fix its main weakness: a sentence beginning “now we know” can pressure people to invent a benefit or endorse an unsupported conclusion.

Prepare slips with three equally prominent choices: “Something became clearer,” “A question remains,” and “I am disappointed and want to leave it here.” An optional second line asks what became clearer or remains unknown. At handback, a volunteer offers the slip once, after explaining the actual outcome. Visitors complete it away from the queue, silently, or decline. Nobody must turn disappointment into learning.

The visitor keeps the slip. A separate, explicit consent box permits copying a short anonymous passage onto the board under “Unfinished attempts, useful observations.” A second volunteer checks consent, identifying details and unsupported claims during a lull. Display only observations and questions, never repair instructions or conclusions about safety. If nothing is offered, leave the board sparse; do not create substitute stories. Existing notes may supply examples only where permission covers that use.

Four volunteers retain their repair roles; one prepares paper, one checks proposed display text, and two provide ordinary service cover. The extra work falls mainly on the reviewer, so contributions wait until service permits review.

Compared with P1’s shared questions, P0 offers a more immediate personal endpoint with less preparation, but risks forced positivity. This change preserves its low burden while making an unrewarding ending legitimate. It assumes visitors find private reflection useful; that remains uncertain.
EXPAND.experiment: Pilot during two comparable short handback periods: ordinary handback and the optional slip. One volunteer observes offers, declines, visible pressure after refusal, and added handback time. Offer everyone the same private exit check: “Did anything become clearer?” and “Did you feel expected to make this sound positive?” Include “prefer not to answer”; count nonresponse separately. Ask slip users whether passing felt easy. Stop offers if refusal prompts persuasion or handbacks begin backing up; resume ordinary handback immediately. Retain only if clearer learning accompanies no apparent increase in embarrassment or service burden; a small pilot cannot establish causation.

EXPAND.title: Upgrade of P1: Open Questions with a bounded response
EXPAND.proposal:
Preserve P1’s collective sense-making mechanism: unresolved repairs contribute legitimate questions to a shared board. Fix its blocking weakness: displaying questions alone can make visitors supply material without receiving evidence that anyone understood it.

Before opening, two volunteers use permitted anonymous notes to prepare at most two nontechnical questions. Beneath each, add a short response with three fields: “What the notes support / What remains unknown / What this café can explain today.” For example, a documented information gap may support explaining what information volunteers found missing, without claiming that obtaining it would have repaired the item. If permissions or evidence are inadequate, use an empty board headed “Questions we can acknowledge today”; do not fabricate examples.

After handback, visitors may read silently or submit a question on paper. Submission does not authorize publication: provide a separate explicit consent box. One designated volunteer reviews submissions during a lull, removes identifying details and excludes technical instructions. For at most two contributions, that volunteer adds a bounded written acknowledgment or explanation within existing café practice. Questions requiring investigation receive “We cannot answer this today,” with no promise of follow-up. The closing ritual is silently adding “Heard today” beside the reviewed questions, without voting or rankings.

P1 spreads learning beyond an individual, but its prerequisite is honest interpretation and its displaced cost is volunteer attention. Cap responses rather than creating an unpaid backlog. Unlike the prior organizational-change route, this changes no service or repair procedure. If a response confuses visitors, cover it, acknowledge the uncertainty to affected readers where feasible, and restore the ordinary verbal explanation.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare a short period with the board available against ordinary handback with the board covered. Use the same optional private exit questions in both: “Can you name something clearer now?” and “Did anything make you feel exposed or judged?” Observe reading, bypassing, submission pressure and reviewer time; check whether visitors understood that participation and publication were separate choices. The designated reviewer stops additions if checking consumes service time or anonymity is doubtful; ordinary service continues. No gain in understandable learning, or increased embarrassment or queue burden, is grounds to drop the added response work.

EXPAND.title: Carry the Learning Forward: an owner-controlled handoff
EXPAND.proposal:
Use continuity as the new mechanism: celebrate an unsuccessful attempt by preserving verified information for a possible next conversation, so the effort need not disappear when the visit ends. The useful outcome is a portable handoff, not a public account or a demand for positive reflection.

Prepare a small paper template: “Reason for visit / What was observed here / What remains unknown / What I want a future helper to understand.” After normal handback, offer an optional copy to the owner. A volunteer may transcribe only observations already recorded in that visit’s repair notes, then let the owner correct the account or leave their final field blank. State “Unresolved; this record does not establish safety.” Include no repair instructions, speculative diagnosis or recommendation to use the item.

The entry threshold is a contemporaneous note that the responsible repair volunteer can verify and the owner agrees may be copied. That volunteer owns the handoff; nobody acts on a diagnosis through this ritual. If verification or time is unavailable, provide a blank owner-written question card explicitly marked “Owner’s account; not checked by the café.” Do not delay departure to complete it.

The owner keeps the only copy and chooses whether to show it elsewhere. No names or photographs are requested. The board carries only the generic statement “Useful observations can travel with an unfinished repair.” Offering the completed record is the quiet celebration; there is no public story collection.

This differs from P0’s reflective endpoint and P1’s shared uncertainty: its benefit depends on preserving usable continuity. It assumes some owners anticipate another conversation. Its costs are transcription time, possible distress from repeating the story, and misplaced authority attached to written notes. If an error is noticed before departure, correct or replace the card with the owner; if it cannot be resolved, remove the disputed passage and provide the blank alternative.
EXPAND.experiment: Offer the handoff during one short period and use ordinary handback during another. The responsible volunteer caps completion at roughly one minute outside the queue. An optional private check asks owners to identify one confirmed observation and one remaining uncertainty, then whether the exchange felt useful, embarrassing or burdensome. Observe corrections, declines, opt-out ease and volunteer time. Stop immediately if cards are interpreted as safety clearance, errors recur, or service slows; return to ordinary handback and replace affected cards while their owners are present. This tests immediate understanding and dignity, not whether a future repair succeeds.
